subtopic_detail: Declaring serotonergic treatment failure in body dysmorphic disorder before the dose has been optimised
stem:
You are the psychiatry registrar reviewing a 23-year-old man who was referred twelve months ago and has been under the care of the clinic since. He tells you he spends 'three or four hours a day' checking his nose in reflective surfaces and comparing it with photographs of other men, and that he believes it is crooked and bulbous.

He has stopped attending tutorials, sits at the back of buses and will only meet friends in dim venues. He has consulted two cosmetic surgeons and underwent a rhinoplasty eighteen months ago, after which he felt the appearance was worse.

On examination his nose has a normal contour with a well healed surgical scar and no deformity. He has taken sertraline 50 mg daily for the past twelve months, which he confirms he takes every morning without missing doses, and he reports no change in the checking or the distress. He has had no adverse effects from the medication and has never had a trial of any other treatment.

data_table.Mental state: Preoccupation with the appearance of the nose held with poor but not absent insight; no perceptual disturbance; no suicidal plan
data_table.Behaviour: Three to four hours daily mirror checking and photographic comparison; avoidance of tutorials, public transport seating and bright venues
data_table.Examination: Nose of normal contour with a well healed surgical scar and no deformity
data_table.Current treatment: Sertraline 50 mg orally daily for twelve months, taken consistently, no adverse effects, no other treatment trialled

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in his treatment?

options.text: Refer him to a plastic surgeon for a further surgical opinion about his nose
options.rationale: Cosmetic procedures in body dysmorphic disorder leave the preoccupation unchanged or worse in the great majority of cases, and his own experience after rhinoplasty demonstrates exactly that. Surgery would be appropriate only if there were an objective deformity, and his nose has a normal contour. (Source: RANZCP: Obsessive compulsive and related disorders)
source_refs: RANZCP: Obsessive compulsive and related disorders

options.text: Switch him to low dose olanzapine and review his response in eight weeks
options.rationale: An antipsychotic is used as augmentation when beliefs are held with delusional conviction and a properly dosed serotonergic trial has failed, not as a substitute for optimising that trial. His insight is poor rather than absent, which does not by itself change first-line treatment. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

options.text: Increase the sertraline towards 200 mg daily and review after twelve weeks
options.rationale: Body dysmorphic disorder characteristically requires serotonergic doses at the upper end of the range, comparable to those used in obsessive compulsive disorder, and 50 mg of sertraline is a starting dose rather than an adequate trial. An adequate trial is defined as 12 weeks at the maximum tolerated dose, so treatment failure cannot be declared until the dose has been pushed. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

options.text: Stop the sertraline and start a tricyclic antidepressant at a standard dose
options.rationale: Clomipramine is the one tricyclic with evidence in this disorder because of its potent serotonin reuptake inhibition, and other tricyclics have none. Switching agents before optimising the current one also loses whatever partial response has accrued. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

options.text: Stop the sertraline and arrange supportive counselling with his practitioner
options.rationale: Generic supportive counselling has no evidence in body dysmorphic disorder, which responds to a specifically structured cognitive behavioural therapy with exposure and response prevention and perceptual retraining. Withdrawing medication at the same time removes the one active treatment he is receiving. (Source: RANZCP: Obsessive compulsive and related disorders)
source_refs: RANZCP: Obsessive compulsive and related disorders

explanation.summary: Body dysmorphic disorder is a preoccupation with one or more perceived defects in physical appearance that are not observable or appear slight to others, accompanied by repetitive behaviours such as mirror checking, grooming, skin picking, reassurance seeking or comparing. It is under-recognised because sufferers present to dermatologists and cosmetic surgeons rather than to mental health services, and insight is frequently poor, with a substantial minority holding their beliefs with delusional conviction. Suicidality is high, exceeding that seen in obsessive compulsive disorder and major depression, so risk is assessed at every review. Treatment combines a specifically adapted cognitive behavioural therapy with a serotonin reuptake inhibitor, and the doses required are consistently higher and the time to response longer than in depression, which is why premature dose-limited trials are the commonest reason for apparent treatment resistance. Cosmetic intervention rarely satisfies the concern and often shifts it to another body area.
key_points: The perceived defect is absent or slight to an observer, while the distress and time cost are large
Serotonergic doses must reach the upper end of the range, as in obsessive compulsive disorder
An adequate trial is 12 weeks at the maximum tolerated dose before declaring failure
Suicide risk is higher than in obsessive compulsive disorder or major depression
Cosmetic procedures usually leave the preoccupation unchanged or displaced elsewhere
explanation.pearls: Muscle dysmorphia, the belief that the body is insufficiently muscular, is a specifier of body dysmorphic disorder that occurs almost entirely in men and carries a high rate of anabolic androgenic steroid use, so ask directly about supplement and injectable use.

sources.label: RANZCP: Obsessive compulsive and related disorders
BMJ Best Practice: Body dysmorphic disorder

subtopic_detail: First-line intervention for electronic gaming machine losses disclosed during a consultation for insomnia
stem:
You are the general practice registrar seeing a 41-year-old man who booked in for 'something to help me sleep'. He has been lying awake until 3 am for several months and has lost 6 kg without trying.

When you ask what keeps him awake he discloses that he has lost about 60,000 dollars on electronic gaming machines over two years. He describes returning the next day to win back what he has lost, telling his wife he is working late, and taking a redraw on the mortgage that she does not know about. He says he has tried to stop 'at least ten times' and lasts a week.

He drinks two standard drinks on a Friday and uses no other substances. He scores 8 on the Patient Health Questionnaire 9 with no suicidal ideation on direct questioning, and describes his low mood as entirely tied to the financial situation. He has never sought help for gambling and does not know what services exist.

data_table.Mental state: Mood reactive and tied to financial stress, Patient Health Questionnaire 9 score of 8, no suicidal ideation on direct questioning
data_table.Gambling history: Approximately 60,000 dollars lost on electronic gaming machines over two years; chasing losses; concealment from family; mortgage redraw; ten failed attempts to stop
data_table.Substance use: Two standard drinks weekly, no other substance use
data_table.Physical: Unintentional 6 kg weight loss, initial insomnia to 3 am

options.text: Start naltrexone 50 mg daily and review his gambling again in eight weeks
options.rationale: Opioid antagonists have modest evidence in gambling disorder and are considered when structured psychological therapy has failed or when there is a strong family history of alcohol use disorder. Starting a drug before any psychological or financial intervention inverts the treatment hierarchy. (Source: RANZCP: Gambling disorder)

options.text: Refer for gambling specific psychological therapy with financial counselling
options.rationale: Cognitive behavioural therapy addressing the erroneous beliefs about randomness and near misses, combined with financial counselling to restructure access to money, is first line and is available free through Gambling Help services in every Australian state. Addressing the debt is part of treatment rather than separate from it, because unmanaged financial pressure is itself a driver of chasing behaviour and of suicide risk. (Source: RANZCP: Gambling disorder)

options.text: Start sertraline 50 mg daily and review his gambling again in eight weeks
options.rationale: Antidepressants treat a comorbid depressive disorder but do not reduce gambling behaviour in their own right, and his low mood is described as entirely reactive to the financial situation. Treating the mood alone would leave the behaviour and the debt untouched. (Source: RANZCP: Gambling disorder)

options.text: Advise venue self-exclusion alone and review his gambling again in eight weeks
options.rationale: Self-exclusion is a useful adjunct that reduces access to particular venues, but it is readily circumvented, does not cover online platforms, and does nothing about the cognitions that sustain the behaviour. It belongs within a treatment plan rather than as the whole of it. (Source: RANZCP: Gambling disorder)

options.text: Refer him to a residential withdrawal unit for a supervised admission this week
options.rationale: Residential withdrawal exists to manage the physiological withdrawal syndromes of alcohol, opioids and benzodiazepines, and gambling has no such syndrome requiring medical supervision. He drinks two standard drinks weekly and uses no other substances. (Source: RANZCP: Gambling disorder)

explanation.summary: Gambling disorder is classified among the substance related and addictive disorders because it shares the reward pathway, tolerance and withdrawal-like features of substance dependence, and in Australia electronic gaming machines account for the majority of harm. It is almost never the presenting complaint, surfacing instead through insomnia, anxiety, depression, relationship breakdown or financial crisis, so asking about gambling directly is what makes the diagnosis. The diagnostic features to elicit are preoccupation, escalating stakes to achieve the same excitement, repeated failed attempts to cut down, chasing losses, lying to conceal involvement, and jeopardising relationships or employment. Suicide risk is substantially elevated and rises sharply at moments of financial disclosure or crisis, so it is asked about at every contact. First-line treatment is cognitive behavioural therapy targeting erroneous cognitions about randomness, combined with financial counselling and practical restriction of access to funds, with pharmacotherapy reserved for non-response.
key_points: Gambling presents through insomnia, mood, relationship or financial problems rather than directly
Ask about preoccupation, escalation, chasing losses, concealment and failed attempts to stop
Cognitive behavioural therapy plus financial counselling is first line
Free state-based Gambling Help services provide both components
Suicide risk is elevated and peaks around financial disclosure and crisis
explanation.pearls: Ask specifically about dopamine agonists in any patient with new onset gambling: pramipexole and ropinirole prescribed for Parkinson disease or restless legs cause impulse control disorders in up to 17 per cent of users, and the behaviour resolves when the drug is withdrawn.

subtopic_detail: Consistent failure to speak at school with fluent speech at home for more than a year
stem:
You are the psychiatry registrar in a child and adolescent clinic seeing a 6-year-old girl referred by her school. The teacher's report says she has not spoken a single word in the classroom or playground in the fourteen months since she started school, and communicates by nodding, pointing and writing.

Her mother says she 'never stops talking' at home, tells long stories, argues with her older brother and sings loudly. A recording made at home and played in the clinic confirms fluent, well structured speech with age appropriate vocabulary and articulation.

At her school entry health check her hearing was normal on audiometry. She makes eye contact with you, smiles at her mother, shares a drawing spontaneously and plays imaginatively with the clinic dolls, and her teacher reports she has two friends she plays with silently at lunchtime. She freezes and looks at the floor when the teacher addresses her directly in front of the class.

data_table.School report: No speech in class or playground for 14 months; communicates by nodding, pointing and writing; freezes when addressed in front of the class
data_table.Home observation: Fluent, well structured, age appropriate speech confirmed on a home recording
data_table.Social development: Eye contact maintained, shared enjoyment with mother, spontaneous showing behaviour, imaginative doll play, two reciprocal friendships
data_table.Investigations: Audiometry at school entry within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Arrange audiological assessment before any other referral is considered
options.rationale: Hearing assessment is essential in any child with reduced speech output and has already been done with a normal result at school entry. Repeating it delays treatment and cannot explain speech that is fluent at home and absent at school. (Source: RANZCP: Child and adolescent anxiety disorders)
source_refs: RANZCP: Child and adolescent anxiety disorders

options.text: Start fluoxetine and review her speech at school again in twelve weeks
options.rationale: A serotonin reuptake inhibitor is added when a structured behavioural programme has been properly delivered and has not produced progress, or when the impairment is severe and entrenched. Medication as the opening move skips the intervention with the strongest evidence in this age group. (Source: RANZCP: Child and adolescent anxiety disorders)
source_refs: RANZCP: Child and adolescent anxiety disorders

options.text: Refer for an autism spectrum diagnostic assessment before any treatment
options.rationale: Reduced speech at school would raise this question, but she maintains eye contact, shows spontaneous sharing, plays imaginatively and sustains reciprocal friendships, all of which argue against a pervasive social communication difficulty. The selectivity of the mutism by setting is itself the discriminating feature. (Source: RANZCP: Child and adolescent anxiety disorders)
source_refs: RANZCP: Child and adolescent anxiety disorders

options.text: Refer for graded exposure behavioural therapy delivered with the school
options.rationale: Consistent failure to speak in specific social situations despite speaking fluently elsewhere, persisting beyond a month of school and interfering with education, is selective mutism, an anxiety disorder rather than a language or oppositional problem. Behavioural treatment using stimulus fading and graded exposure delivered jointly by clinician, family and school is first line, and early intervention prevents the pattern becoming entrenched. (Source: RANZCP: Child and adolescent anxiety disorders)
source_refs: RANZCP: Child and adolescent anxiety disorders

options.text: Advise the school to wait and review her speech again in twelve months
options.rationale: A brief settling-in period of up to a month after starting school is expected and does not warrant diagnosis, which is why the criteria require a duration beyond one month. Fourteen months of complete mutism is well past that point, and delay is associated with poorer outcomes. (Source: RANZCP: Child and adolescent anxiety disorders)
source_refs: RANZCP: Child and adolescent anxiety disorders

explanation.summary: Selective mutism is classified as an anxiety disorder and is defined by consistent failure to speak in specific social situations where speaking is expected, despite speaking normally in others, for at least one month beyond the first month of school. It is commonly misread as shyness, wilful refusal, a language disorder or autism, and the delay to referral averages several years, which matters because outcomes are better with earlier intervention. The diagnostic work is largely exclusionary: confirm normal hearing, confirm fluent age appropriate speech in at least one setting, and confirm that social reciprocity is intact outside the feared situations. Comorbid social anxiety disorder is present in the majority, and a smaller group has a coexisting speech or language difficulty that warrants its own assessment. Treatment is behavioural, using stimulus fading, shaping and graded exposure delivered collaboratively across home, clinic and classroom, with a serotonin reuptake inhibitor reserved for severe or treatment resistant cases.
key_points: Speech is fluent in at least one setting, which distinguishes this from a language disorder
Duration must exceed one month beyond the first month of schooling
Preserved eye contact, shared enjoyment and imaginative play argue against autism spectrum disorder
Behavioural therapy with school involvement is first line; medication is second line
Most children have comorbid social anxiety disorder, which is treated at the same time
explanation.pearls: Pressing a mute child to speak, or rewarding a single word in front of the class, reliably worsens the avoidance; the effective technique is stimulus fading, in which a new person is gradually introduced into a setting where the child is already speaking comfortably.

sources.label: RANZCP: Child and adolescent anxiety disorders

subtopic_detail: Choosing ADHD pharmacotherapy in an adult with concurrent methamphetamine use
stem:
You are the psychiatry registrar seeing a 30-year-old man referred for assessment of attention difficulties. He says he 'cannot hold a thought long enough to finish anything' and has been dismissed from three jobs in two years for missed deadlines and lateness.

His primary school reports, which he brings with him, document inattention, fidgeting and disrupted classwork from Year 2 onwards, well before the age of 12. His partner confirms current difficulties with organisation, losing possessions and interrupting, present across work, home and social settings.

He uses methamphetamine by smoking it two to three times a week and has done so for about four years, describing it as 'the only thing that gets me through a shift'. He has no psychotic symptoms now and has never had any. He drinks alcohol rarely, has a normal physical examination, a blood pressure of 124/78 mmHg and a normal electrocardiogram.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 78/min, blood pressure 124/78 mmHg, respiratory rate 14/min, SpO2 99 per cent on room air, temperature 36.7°C
data_table.Developmental history: Primary school reports documenting inattention and hyperactivity from Year 2, before age 12
data_table.Current impairment: Organisation, losing possessions and interrupting across work, home and social settings; three job losses in two years
data_table.Substance use: Methamphetamine smoked two to three times weekly for four years; alcohol rarely; no psychotic symptoms ever
data_table.Investigations: Physical examination and electrocardiogram within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management plan?

options.text: Start atomoxetine and refer him concurrently to a drug and alcohol service
options.rationale: Australian guidance is explicit that ADHD treatment should not be withheld while a substance use disorder is addressed, because untreated ADHD worsens substance use outcomes, and the two are treated concurrently. A non-stimulant such as atomoxetine has no misuse or diversion liability and is preferred while methamphetamine use is active, with a long-acting stimulant considered once use is stable. (Source: Australian Evidence-Based Clinical Practice Guideline for ADHD)
source_refs: Australian Evidence-Based Clinical Practice Guideline for ADHD

options.text: Start immediate release dexamfetamine and refer him to a drug service
options.rationale: Immediate release stimulants have the highest misuse and diversion potential of the available options and share a pharmacological class with the drug he is already using. If a stimulant is used at all in this setting it is a long-acting preparation, and only once the substance use is stable. (Source: Australian Evidence-Based Clinical Practice Guideline for ADHD)
source_refs: Australian Evidence-Based Clinical Practice Guideline for ADHD

options.text: Withhold all ADHD treatment until he has been abstinent for six months
options.rationale: Requiring abstinence before treatment is an outdated position that the Australian guideline specifically rejects, since untreated ADHD is itself a driver of continued substance use and of attrition from drug and alcohol services. Abstinence is a goal of the concurrent treatment, not a precondition for it. (Source: Australian Evidence-Based Clinical Practice Guideline for ADHD)
source_refs: Australian Evidence-Based Clinical Practice Guideline for ADHD

options.text: Refer him to a drug and alcohol service and defer the ADHD diagnosis
options.rationale: Deferring the diagnosis would be defensible if the only evidence of inattention came from the period of substance use, since stimulant use can mimic the symptom profile. Contemporaneous school reports documenting symptoms from Year 2 establish onset well before age 12 and before any drug exposure. (Source: Australian Evidence-Based Clinical Practice Guideline for ADHD)
source_refs: Australian Evidence-Based Clinical Practice Guideline for ADHD

options.text: Start a sedating antipsychotic and refer him to a drug and alcohol service
options.rationale: Antipsychotics have a role in methamphetamine induced psychosis and in acute behavioural disturbance, and he has never had psychotic symptoms. They do not treat inattention and carry metabolic and extrapyramidal burden without benefit here. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

explanation.summary: Adult ADHD requires several symptoms to have been present before the age of 12, impairment in two or more settings, and symptoms not better explained by another disorder, and the childhood onset criterion is the one that substance use most often obscures. Collateral evidence from school reports, parents or a long-term partner is therefore central to the assessment rather than optional. Substance use disorders are two to three times more common in adults with ADHD than in the general population, and the relationship runs both ways, with untreated ADHD predicting earlier onset and poorer treatment retention. The Australian guideline recommends treating both conditions concurrently rather than sequentially, favouring non-stimulants or long-acting stimulant formulations where diversion or misuse is a concern. Stimulant prescribing for adults in Australia additionally requires a state or territory authority and is generally initiated by a psychiatrist, and driving and occupational implications are discussed at initiation.
key_points: Childhood onset before age 12 must be established, ideally with contemporaneous collateral evidence
Treat ADHD and substance use disorder concurrently; abstinence is not a precondition
Non-stimulants and long-acting stimulants are preferred where misuse or diversion is a concern
Immediate release stimulants carry the highest diversion potential
Adult stimulant prescribing in Australia requires a state authority and usually psychiatrist initiation
explanation.pearls: Atomoxetine takes 4 to 6 weeks to reach full effect, unlike stimulants which work within hours, so patients must be warned in advance or they will discontinue it in the second week believing it has failed.

sources.label: Australian Evidence-Based Clinical Practice Guideline for ADHD

subtopic_detail: Consent for continuing maintenance electroconvulsive therapy when a family member objects
stem:
You are the psychiatry registrar in a clinic reviewing a 74-year-old woman who has had four episodes of severe depression with psychotic features over eleven years. Each episode involved food and fluid refusal and nihilistic delusions, and each remitted with a course of electroconvulsive therapy after failing two adequate antidepressant trials.

For the past nine months she has received maintenance electroconvulsive therapy every four weeks alongside nortriptyline and has remained well, living independently and driving to her grandchildren's school.

Today she tells you she wants to continue the treatments because 'they are the only thing that has ever kept me out of hospital'. She describes the memory gaps around treatment days, the anaesthetic risks and the alternative of medication alone, and explains why she accepts the trade-off. She scores 27 out of 30 on the Montreal Cognitive Assessment. Her adult son telephoned before the appointment saying he wants the treatment stopped because he has read that it causes brain damage.

data_table.Mental state: Euthymic, no psychotic features, no suicidal ideation, insight into the illness and the treatment intact
data_table.Capacity assessment: Retains, understands, weighs and communicates the risks, benefits and alternatives of the treatment
data_table.Treatment history: Four episodes of psychotic depression over 11 years, each remitting with electroconvulsive therapy after two failed antidepressant trials; well for 9 months on four weekly maintenance treatment plus nortriptyline
data_table.Family position: Adult son telephoned requesting that treatment be stopped

lead_in: What is the most appropriate course of action?

options.text: Defer the treatment until her son agrees to the maintenance programme
options.rationale: A relative has no legal authority to veto treatment for an adult with decision-making capacity, and deferring on that basis would expose her to relapse of an illness that has previously involved food and fluid refusal. Family concerns are addressed by discussion with her consent, not by suspending her treatment. (Source: RANZCP: Electroconvulsive therapy)

options.text: Apply to the guardianship tribunal for a substitute decision maker now
options.rationale: Substitute decision making processes are engaged only when a person lacks capacity for the decision in question. Invoking a tribunal for a woman who demonstrably retains capacity removes her rights rather than protecting them. (Source: RANZCP: Electroconvulsive therapy)

options.text: Stop the maintenance treatment and continue nortriptyline as monotherapy
options.rationale: Antidepressant monotherapy has already failed to prevent four episodes, and relapse rates after a successful acute course are substantially higher without maintenance electroconvulsive therapy in this group. Stopping would also be a unilateral decision against the expressed wish of a capacitous patient. (Source: RANZCP: Electroconvulsive therapy)

options.text: Ask her son to sign the consent form on her behalf before proceeding
options.rationale: Consent signed by another person is valid only where that person holds a formal substitute decision making role and the patient lacks capacity. Obtaining a relative's signature for a capacitous adult is legally ineffective and would invalidate the consent. (Source: RANZCP: Electroconvulsive therapy)

options.text: Proceed on her own informed consent and document the capacity assessment
options.rationale: She retains, understands, weighs and communicates the relevant information, which satisfies the test for decision-making capacity, and consent for electroconvulsive therapy in Australia rests with the patient whenever capacity is present. The right response to the son's concern is to offer, with her permission, a discussion of the actual evidence on cognitive effects, while documenting the capacity assessment and re-confirming consent before each treatment. (Source: RANZCP: Electroconvulsive therapy)

explanation.summary: Electroconvulsive therapy is the most effective acute treatment for severe depression with psychotic features, with remission rates well above those of antidepressant pharmacotherapy, and relapse after a successful acute course is high enough that maintenance treatment is offered to patients with a recurrent pattern. Consent is specific to the procedure, must be informed and voluntary, and is reconfirmed before each treatment rather than obtained once for an open-ended course. Capacity is decision-specific and time-specific, and is assessed against whether the person can understand and retain the relevant information, weigh it in arriving at a decision, and communicate that decision. Where capacity is absent, each Australian state and territory has its own statutory pathway, typically involving a mental health tribunal or guardianship body rather than family consent, and these differ enough that local legislation must be checked. The documented cognitive effect is anterograde and retrograde amnesia around the treatment period, which improves over weeks to months and is reduced by right unilateral ultrabrief pulse electrode placement.
key_points: Capacity is decision-specific: understanding, retaining, weighing and communicating
A relative cannot consent for, or veto treatment for, a capacitous adult
Consent for electroconvulsive therapy is reconfirmed before each treatment in a course
Maintenance treatment substantially reduces relapse after a successful acute course
Where capacity is absent, a statutory tribunal pathway applies, and it varies between states
explanation.pearls: Right unilateral ultrabrief pulse placement produces markedly less retrograde amnesia than bitemporal placement but needs stimulation at around six times seizure threshold to match its efficacy, which is why an inadequately dosed unilateral course is a common reason for apparent non-response.

sources.label: BMJ Best Practice: Depression in adults
